title: Die hagere Liese
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 168. Text from Wikisource („Die hagere Liese (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: This tale is the deliberate companion piece to “Der faule Heinz” (Lazy Heinz), not a variant of it: where that tale's Heinz is content to do nothing at all, lean Lisa wears herself and her husband threadbare with restless scheming for a cow she never gets. Grimm sets the two side by side as opposite ways of ruining a marriage, laziness against grasping industry, and neither comes off well.

sentences.t: Ganz anders als der faule Heinz und die dicke Trine, die sich von nichts aus ihrer Ruhe bringen ließen, dachte die hagere Liese.
sentences.l: Quite otherwise than lazy Heinz and fat Trine, who let themselves be brought out of their rest by nothing, thought lean Liese.
sentences.i: Lean Liese thought quite otherwise than lazy Heinz and fat Trine, who let nothing whatever disturb their rest.
sentences.n: The whole comparison comes first and the subject last: German holds the verb in second place — “dachte” — and lets “die hagere Liese” arrive at the very end, so the reader learns how she thought before learning who she was. Liese is a name, the short form of Elisabeth, and not the adverb leise, softly. hager is lean, gaunt, spare. Lazy Heinz and fat Trine are the couple of an earlier tale in this collection, and this one is built as their mirror image.

sentences.t: Sie äscherte sich ab von Morgen bis Abend und lud ihrem Mann, dem langen Lenz, so viel Arbeit auf, daß er schwerer zu tragen hatte als ein Esel an drei Säcken.
sentences.l: She worked herself to ashes from morning till evening and loaded onto her man, long Lenz, so much work that he had heavier to carry than a donkey with three sacks.
sentences.i: She wore herself to a shadow from morning till evening, and piled so much work on her man, long Lenz, that he had a heavier load to carry than a donkey with three sacks.
sentences.n: sich abäschern is literally to burn oneself down to ashes — an old and strong word for wearing oneself out, where modern German would say sich abrackern. aufladen is separable and its particle auf stands at the end of the clause: “lud … auf”. “dem langen Lenz” is dative because it stands in apposition to “ihrem Mann”; lang of a person means tall and lanky, not long. daß is the 1857 spelling of dass and will appear on every page.

sentences.t: Es war aber alles umsonst, sie hatten nichts und kamen zu nichts.
sentences.l: It was however all in vain, they had nothing and came to nothing.
sentences.i: But it was all in vain: they had nothing and came to nothing.
sentences.n: “zu nichts kommen” is to get nowhere, to come to nothing — one of the rare idioms that falls out the same way in both languages. umsonst here is in vain; the same word also means free of charge, and only the sentence around it decides which.

sentences.t: Eines Abends, als sie im Bette lag und vor Müdigkeit kaum ein Glied regen konnte, ließen sie die Gedanken doch nicht einschlafen.
sentences.l: One evening, when she lay in bed and for weariness could scarcely stir a limb, the thoughts nevertheless did not let her fall asleep.
sentences.i: One evening, as she lay in bed and could scarcely stir a limb for weariness, her thoughts still would not let her fall asleep.
sentences.n: “Eines Abends” is a bare genitive of time — German needs no preposition where English says “one evening”. “vor Müdigkeit” gives the cause of a state: from weariness, out of weariness. In the main clause the subject is die Gedanken and the object sie: the thoughts do the keeping-awake, and she is what they act on.

sentences.t: Sie stieß ihren Mann mit dem Ellenbogen in die Seite und sprach „hörst du, Lenz, was ich gedacht habe?
sentences.l: She thrust her man with the elbow into the side and spoke “do you hear, Lenz, what I have thought?
sentences.i: She dug her elbow into her man’s side and said: “Listen, Lenz — do you hear what I have been thinking?
sentences.n: German puts the part of the body in a plain prepositional phrase — “stieß ihren Mann … in die Seite” — where English makes it possessive: dug her elbow into his side. “hörst du” at the head of a speech is not a real question but an attention-getter, simply “listen”. sprach is this teller’s verb for said and recurs throughout.

sentences.t: wenn ich einen Gulden fände, und einer mir geschenkt würde, so wollte ich einen dazu borgen, und du solltest mir auch noch einen geben: so bald ich dann die vier Gulden beisammen hätte, so wollte ich eine junge Kuh kaufen.“
sentences.l: if I found a gulden, and one were given me as a present, then I would borrow one to it, and you should give me one more as well: as soon as I then had the four gulden together, then I would buy a young cow.”
sentences.i: if I were to find a gulden, and one were made me as a gift, then I would borrow another to go with them, and you should give me one more besides; and as soon as I had the four gulden together, I would buy a young cow.”
sentences.n: Every verb here stands in the subjunctive of the unreal — fände, würde, wollte, hätte — so the whole plan floats clear of anything that has happened or will. Four gulden: one found, one given, one borrowed and one squeezed out of Lenz. The arithmetic is the joke, since not one of the four exists. Der Gulden was a real silver coin of the German states.

sentences.t: Dem Mann gefiel das recht gut, „ich weiß zwar nicht,“ sprach er, „woher ich den Gulden nehmen soll, den du von mir willst geschenkt haben, aber wenn du dennoch das Geld zusammenbringst, und du kannst dafür eine Kuh kaufen, so thust du wohl, wenn du dein Vorhaben ausführst.
sentences.l: To the man that pleased quite well, “I do not know, to be sure,” spoke he, “from where I am to take the gulden that you want to have given from me, but if you nevertheless bring the money together, and you can buy a cow for it, then you do well if you carry out your intention.
sentences.i: The man liked that well enough. “I do not know, to be sure,” he said, “where I am to get the gulden you want as a gift from me; but if you do bring the money together all the same, and can buy a cow with it, then you will do well to carry out your plan.
sentences.n: gefallen takes the dative of the person pleased: “dem Mann gefiel das” is literally to the man that pleased, where English makes the man the subject. “zwar … aber” pairs an admission with an objection — to be sure … but. thust is the 1857 spelling of tust; thun and its forms keep the h all through this book.

sentences.t: Ich freue mich,“ fügte er hinzu, „wenn die Kuh ein Kälbchen bringt, so werde ich doch manchmal zu meiner Erquickung einen Trunk Milch erhalten.“
sentences.l: I am glad,” added he thereto, “when the cow brings a little calf, then I shall after all sometimes receive a draught of milk for my refreshment.”
sentences.i: I am glad,” he added, “for when the cow brings a calf, I shall get a draught of milk now and then for my refreshment.”
sentences.n: hinzufügen is separable and the particle hinzu goes to the end: “fügte er hinzu”. “zu meiner Erquickung” is a phrase of purpose — for my refreshment. Erquickung is an old and rather solemn word, and Lenz spending it on a mouthful of milk is part of the comedy.

sentences.t: „Die Milch ist nicht für dich,“ sagte die Frau, „wir lassen das Kalb saugen, damit es groß und fett wird, und wir es gut verkaufen können.“
sentences.l: “The milk is not for you,” said the woman, “we let the calf suck, so that it becomes big and fat, and we can sell it well.”
sentences.i: “The milk is not for you,” said the woman. “We let the calf suckle, so that it grows big and fat and we can sell it for a good price.”
sentences.n: dich is the accusative of du and is simply you — the couples in this book address each other with du throughout. damit introduces a clause of purpose and sends its verb to the end: “damit es groß und fett wird”.

sentences.t: „Freilich,“ antwortete der Mann, „aber ein wenig Milch nehmen wir doch, das schadet nichts.“
sentences.l: “To be sure,” answered the man, “but a little milk we take after all, that harms nothing.”
sentences.i: “To be sure,” answered the man, “but we will take a little milk all the same — that does no harm.”
sentences.n: doch is one of the small words German leans on a sentence with; here it quietly insists — we will take some anyway. Fronting the object, “ein wenig Milch nehmen wir”, puts the milk first and the subject after the verb, which German can do with almost any element.

sentences.t: „Wer hat dich gelehrt mit Kühen umgehen?“ sprach die Frau, „es mag schaden oder nicht, ich will es nicht haben: und wenn du dich auf den Kopf stellst, du kriegst keinen Tropfen Milch.
sentences.l: “Who has taught you to deal with cows?” spoke the woman, “it may harm or not, I will not have it: and if you place yourself on the head, you get not a drop of milk.
sentences.i: “Who taught you how to handle cows?” said the woman. “Harm or no harm, I will not have it — and if you stand on your head, you shall not get a drop of milk.
sentences.n: “sich auf den Kopf stellen” is to stand on one’s head, said of doing everything imaginable: however you carry on, it will make no difference. lehren takes a bare infinitive here, “gelehrt … umgehen”, where modern German would put zu in front of it. kriegen is the everyday word for to get.

sentences.t: Du langer Lenz, weil du nicht zu ersättigen bist, meinst du du wolltest verzehren was ich mit Mühe erwerbe.“
sentences.l: You long Lenz, because you are not to be satisfied, you think you would consume what I with effort earn.”
sentences.i: You lanky Lenz — because you are never to be filled, you think you may eat up what I earn with such labour.”
sentences.n: “nicht zu ersättigen sein” is the passive of possibility built with sein + zu + infinitive: not to be satisfied, that is, impossible to fill. lang of a person is tall and lanky, and she throws it at him as an insult. wolltest is subjunctive — what he supposes he would be allowed to do.

sentences.t: „Frau,“ sagte der Mann, „sei still, oder ich hänge dir eine Maultasche an.“
sentences.l: “Wife,” said the man, “be quiet, or I hang you a slap-in-the-mouth on.”
sentences.i: “Wife,” said the man, “be quiet, or I shall fetch you a slap in the face.”
sentences.n: “jemandem eine Maultasche anhängen” is an old idiom for fetching someone a blow across the mouth; anhängen is separable and its particle an waits at the end of the clause. Frau as a form of address is simply wife. sei is the imperative of sein.

sentences.t: „Was,“ rief sie, „du willst mir drohen, du Nimmersatt, du Strick, du fauler Heinz.“
sentences.l: “What,” cried she, “you want to threaten me, you Never-full, you rope, you lazy Heinz.”
sentences.i: “What!” she cried. “You mean to threaten me — you glutton, you rogue, you lazy Heinz.”
sentences.n: Nimmersatt is built straight out of nimmer and satt, never-full: a glutton. Strick is a rope, and as abuse a rogue, one fit for the gallows. Her worst insult is to call him by the name of the laziest man in the book — the tale opened by measuring the two couples against each other, and she closes the circle herself.

sentences.t: Sie wollte ihm in die Haare fallen, aber der lange Lenz richtete sich auf, packte mit der einen Hand die dürren Arme der hagern Liese zusammen,
sentences.l: She wanted to fall to him into the hair, but the long Lenz raised himself up, packed with the one hand the withered arms of lean Liese together,
sentences.i: She would have flown at his hair, but long Lenz raised himself up, gathered lean Liese’s scrawny arms together in one hand,
sentences.n: “jemandem in die Haare fallen” is to fly at someone, to go for them, with the dative ihm marking whose hair. zusammenpacken is separable and its particle waits at the end: “packte … zusammen”. hagern is the weak inflection of hager after the article.

sentences.t: mit der andern drückte er ihr den Kopf auf das Kissen, ließ sie schimpfen und hielt sie so lange bis sie vor großer Müdigkeit eingeschlafen war.
sentences.l: with the other he pressed her the head onto the pillow, let her rail and held her so long until she from great weariness had fallen asleep.
sentences.i: and with the other he pressed her head down on the pillow, let her rail on, and held her until she had fallen asleep from sheer weariness.
sentences.n: “drückte ihr den Kopf” is the dative of possession: German says pressed the head to her where English says pressed her head. lassen with a bare infinitive, “ließ sie schimpfen”, is to let a thing go on. Nothing is softened here — the quarrel ends with him simply holding her down until she gives out.

sentences.t: Ob sie am andern Morgen beim Erwachen fortfuhr zu zanken, oder ob sie ausgieng den Gulden zu suchen, den sie finden wollte, das weiß ich nicht.
sentences.l: Whether she the next morning on waking went on to quarrel, or whether she went out to seek the gulden that she wanted to find, that know I not.
sentences.i: Whether she went on quarrelling the next morning when she woke, or whether she went out to look for the gulden she meant to find — that I do not know.
sentences.n: The teller steps forward at the last moment and refuses to finish: “das weiß ich nicht”. weiß here is the verb wissen, to know, and not the adjective weiß, white; the two are spelled alike. ausgieng is the 1857 spelling of ausging, and “beim Erwachen” turns a verb into a noun after a preposition: on waking.

glossary.erhalten: erhalten — to receive, to obtain (infinitive; here with werde, the future: I shall receive)
glossary.es: es — it (neuter pronoun, and the impersonal subject of es war, es gieng)
glossary.fügte: hinzufügen — added (3rd sg. pret.; separable, hinzu at the end: fügte … hinzu)
glossary.hinzu: hinzu — the particle of hinzufügen, to add (fügte er hinzu: he added)
glossary.hänge: anhängen — (I) hang on, fetch (1st sg. pres.; separable, particle an at the end; eine Maultasche anhängen: to fetch someone a slap)
glossary.ihm: ihm — to him, to it (dative of er and of es)
glossary.langer: lang — long; of a person, tall and lanky (masc. nom. sg.; du langer Lenz: you lanky Lenz)
glossary.liese: Liese — Lisa (woman’s name, short form of Elisabeth; not the adverb leise, softly)
glossary.ließen: lassen — let (3rd pl. pret.; sich bringen lassen: to let oneself be brought; einschlafen lassen: to let fall asleep)
glossary.lud: aufladen — loaded on, piled on (3rd sg. pret.; separable, auf at the end; jemandem Arbeit aufladen: to pile work on someone)
glossary.packte: zusammenpacken — gathered together, packed together (3rd sg. pret.; separable, zusammen at the end)
glossary.schaden: schaden — to harm, to do damage (infinitive; es mag schaden oder nicht: it may do harm or not)
glossary.solltest: sollen — you were to, you should (2nd sg. past subjunctive, inside her unreal plan)
glossary.stellst: stellen — (you) place, put (2nd sg. pres.; sich auf den Kopf stellen: to stand on one’s head)
glossary.strick: der Strick — rope, cord; as a term of abuse, a rogue, a gallows-bird
glossary.tropfen: der Tropfen — drop (acc. sg.; keinen Tropfen Milch: not a drop of milk)
glossary.vorhaben: das Vorhaben — plan, intention (noun; ein Vorhaben ausführen: to carry out a plan)
glossary.weiß: wissen — (I) know (1st sg. pres.; the same spelling is also weiß, white)
glossary.werde: werden — (I) shall, will (1st sg. pres., forming the future: so werde ich … erhalten)
